node.title: Re: Why Perl Docs examples do not use strict and warnings often (updated)
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
I was browsing through the Perl Data Structures documentation and noticed that though the document suggests using strict, it's not used in any examples.

Actually, it says "[doc://perldsc#WHY-YOU-SHOULD-ALWAYS-use-strict]".

And what alternative do you suggest? Putting it in every example would make the examples longer and the document harder to read, which is why there's a whole separate section near the start of the document explaining it. Many of the examples also run fine in the absence of [doc://strict] and [doc://warnings]. To clarify, obviously one should still always use strict and warnings. But the documentation does still cater to those who don't. Plus, not every code snippet is intended to be a full program. If a code example were to fail in the presence of use strict; use warnings;, I'd call that a documentation issue. But again, I still don't see any concrete suggestions in this thread.

[doc://perlintro], [https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/programming-perl-4th/9781449321451/|the Camel], [http://modernperlbooks.com/|Modern Perl], and many other resources on learning Perl explain fairly early on why one should always [id://111088]. use v5.12; and up, which is required for many modern features to work, also turns on [doc://strict].

How's someone who's new to Perl supposed to know when some internally provided variable is being used vs when a user created variable is being used in the code?

From context and from trying out the examples.

So just in case this isn't a troll: Feel free to submit patches for cases that you think are unclear.
